data.title: Fortress Biotech's (NASDAQ:FBIO) Solid Earnings Are Supported By Other Strong Factors
data.description:
Fortress Biotech, Inc.'s (NASDAQ:FBIO) earnings announcement last week was disappointing for investors, despite the decent profit numbers. We did some digging and actually think they are being unnecessarily pessimistic.

We've found 21 US stocks that are forecast to pay a dividend yield of over 6% next year. See the full list for free.

Examining Cashflow Against Fortress Biotech's Earnings

Many investors haven't heard of the accrual ratio from cashflow, but it is actually a useful measure of how well a company's profit is backed up by free cash flow (FCF) during a given period. To get the accrual ratio we first subtract FCF from profit for a period, and then divide that number by the average operating assets for the period. You could think of the accrual ratio from cashflow as the 'non-FCF profit ratio'.

Therefore, it's actually considered a good thing when a company has a negative accrual ratio, but a bad thing if its accrual ratio is positive. While it's not a problem to have a positive accrual ratio, indicating a certain level of non-cash profits, a high accrual ratio is arguably a bad thing, because it indicates paper profits are not matched by cash flow. Notably, there is some academic evidence that suggests that a high accrual ratio is a bad sign for near-term profits, generally speaking.

For the year to September 2026, Fortress Biotech had an accrual ratio of -0.82. That indicates that its free cash flow quite significantly exceeded its statutory profit. To wit, it produced free cash flow of US$126m during the period, dwarfing its reported profit of US$91.8m. Notably, Fortress Biotech had negative free cash flow last year, so the US$126m it produced this year was a welcome improvement. Unfortunately for shareholders, the company has also been issuing new shares, diluting their share of future earnings.

That might leave you wondering what analysts are forecasting in terms of future profitability. Luckily, you can click here to see an interactive graph depicting future profitability, based on their estimates.

One essential aspect of assessing earnings quality is to look at how much a company is diluting shareholders. In fact, Fortress Biotech increased the number of shares on issue by 7.5% over the last twelve months by issuing new shares. That means its earnings are split among a greater number of shares. To talk about net income, without noticing earnings per share, is to be distracted by the big numbers while ignoring the smaller numbers that talk to per share value. You can see a chart of Fortress Biotech's EPS by clicking here.

A Look At The Impact Of Fortress Biotech's Dilution On Its Earnings Per Share (EPS)

Fortress Biotech was losing money three years ago. Zooming in to the last year, we still can't talk about growth rates coherently, since it made a loss last year. But mathematics aside, it is always good to see when a formerly unprofitable business come good (though we accept profit would have been higher if dilution had not been required). Therefore, the dilution is having a noteworthy influence on shareholder returns.

In the long term, if Fortress Biotech's earnings per share can increase, then the share price should too. However, if its profit increases while its earnings per share stay flat (or even fall) then shareholders might not see much benefit. For that reason, you could say that EPS is more important that net income in the long run, assuming the goal is to assess whether a company's share price might grow.

Our Take On Fortress Biotech's Profit Performance

In conclusion, Fortress Biotech has a strong cashflow relative to earnings, which indicates good quality earnings, but the dilution means its earnings per share are dropping faster than its profit. Based on these factors, we think that Fortress Biotech's profits are a reasonably conservative guide to its underlying profitability. With this in mind, we wouldn't consider investing in a stock unless we had a thorough understanding of the risks. data.title: Why You Might Be Interested In Voya Financial, Inc. (NYSE:VOYA) For Its Upcoming Dividend
data.description:
Some investors rely on dividends for growing their wealth, and if you're one of those dividend sleuths, you might be intrigued to know that Voya Financial, Inc. (NYSE:VOYA) is about to go ex-dividend in just three days. The ex-dividend date is one business day before the record date, which is the cut-off date for shareholders to be present on the company's books to be eligible for a dividend payment. The ex-dividend date is of consequence because whenever a stock is bought or sold, the trade takes at least one business day to settle. Accordingly, Voya Financial investors that purchase the stock on or after the 24th of November will not receive the dividend, which will be paid on the 29th of December.

The company's upcoming dividend is US$0.57 a share, following on from the last 12 months, when the company distributed a total of US$2.28 per share to shareholders. Calculating the last year's worth of payments shows that Voya Financial has a trailing yield of 2.4% on the current share price of US$96.78. If you buy this business for its dividend, you should have an idea of whether Voya Financial's dividend is reliable and sustainable. So we need to investigate whether Voya Financial can afford its dividend, and if the dividend could grow.

That's why it's comforting to see Voya Financial's earnings have been skyrocketing, up 36% per annum for the past five years.

The main way most investors will assess a company's dividend prospects is by checking the historical rate of dividend growth. In the last 10 years, Voya Financial has lifted its dividend by approximately 50% a year on average. Both per-share earnings and dividends have both been growing rapidly in recent times, which is great to see.

To Sum It Up

Companies like Voya Financial that are growing rapidly and paying out a low fraction of earnings, are usually reinvesting heavily in their business. data.title: Just Four Days Till Gildan Activewear Inc. (TSE:GIL) Will Be Trading Ex-Dividend
data.description:
It looks like Gildan Activewear Inc. (TSE:GIL) is about to go ex-dividend in the next 4 days. Typically, the ex-dividend date is one business day before the record date, which is the date on which a company determines the shareholders eligible to receive a dividend. The ex-dividend date is important because any transaction on a stock needs to have been settled before the record date in order to be eligible for a dividend. Therefore, if you purchase Gildan Activewear's shares on or after the 25th of November, you won't be eligible to receive the dividend, when it is paid on the 21st of December.

The company's upcoming dividend is US$0.249 a share, following on from the last 12 months, when the company distributed a total of US$1.00 per share to shareholders. Last year's total dividend payments show that Gildan Activewear has a trailing yield of 2.9% on the current share price of CA$48.73. We love seeing companies pay a dividend, but it's also important to be sure that laying the golden eggs isn't going to kill our golden goose! So we need to check whether the dividend payments are covered, and if earnings are growing.

We've found 21 US stocks that are forecast to pay a dividend yield of over 6% next year. See the full list for free.

Dividends are usually paid out of company profits, so if a company pays out more than it earned then its dividend is usually at greater risk of being cut. Gildan Activewear is paying out an acceptable 51% of its profit, a common payout level among most companies. A useful secondary check can be to evaluate whether Gildan Activewear generated enough free cash flow to afford its dividend. Luckily it paid out just 19% of its free cash flow last year.

It's encouraging to see that the dividend is covered by both profit and cash flow. This generally suggests the dividend is sustainable, as long as earnings don't drop precipitously.

See our latest analysis for Gildan Activewear

Click here to see the company's payout ratio, plus analyst estimates of its future dividends.

Have Earnings And Dividends Been Growing?

Businesses with shrinking earnings are tricky from a dividend perspective. Investors love dividends, so if earnings fall and the dividend is reduced, expect a stock to be sold off heavily at the same time. Gildan Activewear's earnings per share have fallen at approximately 9.0% a year over the previous five years. Such a sharp decline casts doubt on the future sustainability of the dividend.

The main way most investors will assess a company's dividend prospects is by checking the historical rate of dividend growth. Since the start of our data, 10 years ago, Gildan Activewear has lifted its dividend by approximately 12% a year on average. Growing the dividend payout ratio while earnings are declining can deliver nice returns for a while, but it's always worth checking for when the company can't increase the payout ratio any more - because then the music stops.

The Bottom Line

Has Gildan Activewear got what it takes to maintain its dividend payments? We're not enthused by the declining earnings per share, although at least the company's payout ratio is within a reasonable range, meaning it may not be at imminent risk of a dividend cut. In summary, while it has some positive characteristics, we're not inclined to race out and buy Gildan Activewear today.

If you're not too concerned about Gildan Activewear's ability to pay dividends, you should still be mindful of some of the other risks that this business faces. Every company has risks, and we've spotted 5 warning signs for Gildan Activewear you should know about.

data.title: How This Defense Stock Is Creating Solutions To Modern Warfare
data.description:
By 2027, the US military aims to spend more than US$1 billion on a program to procure hundreds of thousands of drones, highlighting how quickly unmanned systems are becoming part of modern warfare.

Drones are transforming the battlefield.

A small first-person view (FPV) drone, which can cost less than US$10,000, can potentially destroy military assets such as tanks and radar systems worth many times its purchase price. This creates an unusual equation for defense spending where relatively inexpensive weapons can threaten some of the most expensive equipment on the battlefield.

This has led to drone stocks becoming a major focus for investors interested in defense exposure.

This has captured the attention of US defense stock First Breach (FBDT), which is looking to mass-produce two models of drones for military purposes.

Drones are a growing area for defense stocks

According to Grand View Research, the US drone market is expected to grow from US$25.1 billion in 2024 to US$52.5 billion by 2030, equivalent to annual growth of around 13%.

The global market is forecast to expand from approximately US$73 billion to US$163 billion over the same period, representing annual growth of 14.3%. These estimates cover the wider drone industry, including commercial applications, but illustrate the scale of the opportunity as adoption expands.

Military procurement is adding to this demand. The US Drone Dominance programme has allocated US$1.1 billion for prototype orders, with the US Army outlining plans involving approximately 340,000 drones.

First Breach hopes to capture some of this opportunity with two proprietary platforms: the Close-Quarters Strike (CQS) and Long Range Strike (LRS).

The CQS is designed for close-range operations, with a demonstrated range of around 2 kilometres and a 500-gram payload. The LRS targets a range exceeding 20 kilometres and a payload of approximately one kilogram, completing its first test flight in October 2026.

First Breach aims to begin scaled production in Q2 2027, eventually reaching a capacity of more than 2,500 drones per week. However, it has yet to report drone revenue or disclose production orders.

Old-fashioned ammunition still necessary

Although drones might be a critical defense technology, traditional technology like ammunition remains important.

According to First Breach, the US market for ammunition is expected to grow just under 12% per year to US$12.1 billion by 2031. Looking specifically at defense spending, in the recent US Army budget, an extra US$7.3 billion was requested to expand munitions, including ammunition.

First Breach is hoping to take advantage of this growth, increasing its market share and expanding its product lines. The company plans to transition to 24-hour production, increasing production capacity by 175%. This will allow the company to manufacture up to 20 million rounds per month.

Helping this increase is a recent agreement with SAS Ammo, an ammunition retailer and wholesaler, that is popular amongst recreational and competitive shooters as well as law enforcement. Under the agreement, the minimum monthly purchase will increase from 3 million rounds to 8 million rounds for a period of three years.

This growth might start to flow through.

In its recent third-quarter result, revenue from ammunition sales rose to $568,856 from $45,853 a year earlier and was 57% above the $361,357 recorded in the first half of 2026 and nearly six times the $95,353 recorded in the second quarter.

First Breach betting on two sides of modern warfare

First Breach is looking to build a footprint in two fast-growing, critical sections of the defense market.

It starts with its established ammunition business where the company aims to increase output, improve manufacturing scale and expand its customer base both in America and overseas.
